title: The web of life
intro: Every insect is a thread in a great web. If one breaks, the others feel it.

lessons.title: Who eats whom?
lessons.intro: What does a frog eat? What does a bird feed its chicks? Let's follow the trail of food.
lessons.closing: Plants feed insects, and insects feed lots and lots of animals. They're a very important thread in the web!

exercises.prompt: Put the food chain in order, from first to last.
exercises.explanation: The plant comes first, because it makes its food from sunlight; the caterpillar eats its leaves and the bird eats the caterpillar.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Who's making that sound?
exercises.explanation: It's a frog croaking. Frogs sing near water, especially at dusk, and they catch insects with their sticky tongues.

exercises.prompt: Tap the animals that eat insects.
exercises.explanation: Birds, frogs and mantises hunt insects. A grown-up butterfly drinks nectar, and a plant makes its food from sunlight.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Every food chain starts with a ___, which makes its food from the light of the ___.
exercises.explanation: Plants are the only ones in the chain that make their own food, from sunlight; everyone else eats someone else.

exercises.prompt: Match each animal with what it eats.
exercises.explanation: Each one eats something different, and that's what makes a web: the leaf feeds the caterpillar, and the caterpillar feeds the bird.

lessons.title: The flower and the bee
lessons.intro: Flowers and bees are great partners: one gives food and the other carries pollen. Let's see how.
lessons.closing: Every time you eat a fruit, remember it was once a flower visited by an insect. Thank you, pollinators!

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place.
exercises.explanation: The pistil is right in the middle, surrounded by stamens with pollen; the colorful petals go all around, and the stem holds it up from below.

exercises.prompt: Match each part with its job.

pairs.right: Where the fruit and seeds grow
Holds the flower up and brings it water

exercises.explanation: Each part has its task: the petals call the insect, the stamens give it pollen and the pistil receives it to make the fruit.

exercises.prompt: Put in order how the bee pollinates.

steps.label: It reaches a flower, drawn by its color and scent
It drinks nectar and pollen sticks to its hairs
It visits another flower of the same kind and leaves pollen on the pistil

exercises.explanation: First the flower attracts it, then pollen sticks to it while it feeds and, when it visits another flower of the same kind, it leaves pollen on the pistil.

exercises.prompt: Why do flowers have bright colors and a nice scent?
options: To attract the insects that pollinate them
exercises.explanation: From far away, the insect sees the color and smells the scent; when it arrives it finds nectar and, along the way, carries pollen to another flower.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: The bee leaves ___ on another flower's pistil, and that's how the ___ and the seeds form.
exercises.explanation: When pollen reaches the pistil of a flower of the same kind, the flower can turn into a fruit with seeds: that's pollination.

lessons.title: The recyclers
lessons.intro: Every day piles of leaves and branches fall to the forest floor. Why don't they cover everything? Thanks to the recyclers.
lessons.closing: Recyclers turn old things into new soil so more plants can grow. They work for everyone, nonstop!

exercises.prompt: Tap the recyclers.
exercises.explanation: Beetles, fly larvae, ants and fungi eat leftovers and break them down. The dragonfly hunts live insects and the bee pollinates flowers.

exercises.prompt: Put each recycler in its box.
exercises.explanation: Insects have six legs. A fungus isn't an animal and an earthworm is a worm with no legs, but both recycle too.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Recyclers ___ leftovers and turn them into ___ soil.
exercises.explanation: By eating leftovers they break them into smaller and smaller pieces, until they become soil again, with food for plants.

exercises.prompt: What would happen in the forest without recyclers?
options: There would be mountains of leaves and the soil would have less food for plants
exercises.explanation: Nobody would break the leftovers down: they would pile up and never go back to the soil as food for new plants.

exercises.prompt: True or false? A fungus is an insect.
exercises.explanation: False: a fungus has no legs and isn't even an animal; it's a group of its own. But it recycles just like beetles do.

lessons.title: Hide and trick
lessons.intro: Most insects can't fight a bird. So how do they survive? With disguises and tricks!
lessons.closing: Hiding, dressing up or warning: every insect has its trick to stay alive. Now you know how to spot them!

exercises.prompt: Where is the stick insect hiding?
exercises.explanation: Its long, thin, brown body looks like a twig: that's camouflage. That way birds go right past without seeing it.

exercises.prompt: Put each insect in the box for its trick.

sortItems.label: Caterpillar that looks like a twig
Butterfly that copies a bad-tasting one

exercises.explanation: Camouflaged ones look like twigs or leaves; mimics look like another animal that stings or tastes bad; and the ladybug does the opposite: it lets itself be seen as a warning.

exercises.prompt: Match each trick with what it achieves.

pairs.right: Saying “I taste bad, don't eat me”

exercises.explanation: All three tricks do the same job, keeping them from being eaten, but each one works in a different way.

exercises.prompt: On a flower you see a fly with yellow and black stripes. Why does it look like a wasp?
options: To warm up in the sun
So birds think it stings and don't eat it
exercises.explanation: It's mimicry: the flower fly doesn't sting, but birds learn to avoid wasp stripes, so they leave it alone.

exercises.prompt: What does camouflage do for the praying mantis?
options: It hides it from birds and helps it surprise the insects it hunts
It lets others see it from far away
exercises.explanation: Still among the leaves, birds don't see it and insects don't see their hunter until it's too late.

lessons.title: Teamwork
lessons.intro: One ant alone can't build an anthill, but thousands together can. Let's meet the insects that live as a team.
lessons.closing: In a colony everyone does their part and everyone wins. Just like a good class team!

exercises.prompt: Tap the insects that live in colonies.
exercises.explanation: Honey bees, ants, leafcutter ants and termites live in huge families with a queen. Butterflies and grasshoppers live on their own.

exercises.prompt: Match each colony member with its job.

pairs.right: Find food and care for the young

exercises.explanation: They share the work: the queen only lays eggs, so the workers feed her and the young, and the big-headed soldiers guard the entrance.

exercises.prompt: Why does the leafcutter ant cut leaves and take them to its nest?
options: To grow a fungus on them, which is its food
exercises.explanation: The leafcutter ant is a farmer: it can't digest leaves well, so it uses them to grow a fungus in the nest, and eats the fungus.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Some ants ___ aphids, and the aphids give them ___ drops.
exercises.explanation: It's a deal between species: the ants protect the aphids from their enemies and, in return, drink the sweet drops the aphids give off.

exercises.prompt: True or false? Termites live in a colony with a queen and also a king.
exercises.explanation: True: in termite colonies, the queen and king live together in the nest for many years. Bees and ants have no king: only the queen lays the eggs.

lessons.title: If insects disappear
lessons.intro: You already know many threads of the web. What would happen if the insect threads broke?
lessons.closing: Without insects, the whole web goes slack. That's why caring for them means caring for fruit, birds and soil. You can help!

exercises.prompt: Who carries its pollen? Put each plant in its box.
exercises.explanation: Mango, passion fruit, cacao and watermelon flowers need insects to carry their pollen. Corn and rice have flowers without showy petals because the wind carries their pollen.

exercises.prompt: Match them up: if we lost…

pairs.right: There would be few fruits and no chocolate
Leaves and leftovers would pile up
Many birds and frogs would go hungry

exercises.explanation: Each group of insects holds up a part of the web: without it, the part that depended on its work falls apart.

exercises.prompt: Who pollinates the cacao flower, which chocolate comes from?
exercises.explanation: The cacao flower is tiny, and it's visited by tiny midges that fit inside it. Without them, there would be no cacao beans.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: To help insects, we can plant ___ and not spray ___ everywhere.
exercises.explanation: Flowers give nectar and pollen to pollinators, and poison can't tell the difference: it also kills the insects that help us.

exercises.prompt: Why would many birds go hungry without insects?
options: Because they feed their chicks insects
Because insects teach them to fly
exercises.explanation: Caterpillars and other insects are soft and full of nutrients: many birds hunt them to raise their chicks.

exam.title: Unit challenge
exam.intro: Web of life challenge! Show that you know how all the threads are tied together.
exam.closing: Well done, ranger! Now you know that every insect, however small, holds up a thread in the web of life.

exercises.prompt: Put the food chain in order, from first to last.
exercises.explanation: The plant makes its food from sunlight, the grasshopper eats the plant and the frog catches the grasshopper with its tongue.

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place.
exercises.explanation: The pistil, in the middle, receives the pollen; the stamens around it hold it; the petals attract insects and the stem holds the flower up.

exercises.prompt: Where is the stick insect hiding?
exercises.explanation: It's hard to see because it looks like just another twig: that's its camouflage against birds.

exercises.prompt: Listen. Who's making that sound?
exercises.explanation: It's a bee buzzing: the sound comes from its wings, which beat super fast as it flies from flower to flower carrying pollen.

exercises.prompt: Put each one in its box.
exercises.explanation: Bees and butterflies carry pollen while looking for nectar; termites eat dead wood and fungi break down leftovers, so both make new soil.

exercises.prompt: Match each insect with its trick.
exercises.explanation: One hides, one dresses up as something that stings and the other warns with bright colors: three ways not to get eaten.

exercises.prompt: What does the queen do in a bee colony?
options: She defends the nest all by herself
exercises.explanation: The queen lays all the colony's eggs; the workers find food, care for the young and defend the hive.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Pollinators carry ___ from flower to flower, and recyclers turn leftovers into new ___.
exercises.explanation: Thanks to the pollen they carry, flowers make fruit; and thanks to recyclers, leftovers become soil full of food again.

exercises.prompt: Tap the animals that eat insects.
exercises.explanation: Frogs, birds and mantises hunt insects. Bees eat nectar and pollen, and a flower is a plant: it makes its food from sunlight.

exercises.prompt: True or false? If insects disappeared, the whole web of life would feel it.
exercises.explanation: True: there would be fewer fruits, leftovers would pile up and many birds and frogs would go hungry.
